meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'little one, kid' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Listen, kid.
The little one is asleep.

examples.text: Послушай, малыш, у меня есть деловое предложение.
examples.trans: Listen, kid, I've got a business proposal.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

скучать.gloss: to miss, yearn for, feel bored

meanings.en: to miss, yearn for, feel bored
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'кучать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to miss, yearn for, feel bored', paired with 'соскучиться'.

examples.text: Я буду очень скучать по вам.
examples.trans: I will miss you very much.
She misses her hometown.

examples.text: Но вся наша кухня очень скучает без вас!
examples.trans: But our entire kitchen misses you very much!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'along; by; about', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm here about the job.
We're talking on the phone.

examples.text: Это Аракелян. Я по поводу торгового центра.
examples.trans: It's Arakelyan. I'm calling about the shopping centre.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'more; still; yet', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You've still got some.
You'll be sorry!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'foie gras' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: And they even brought out the foie gras.

examples.text: На нашей кухне уже есть новая фуа-гра.
examples.trans: In our kitchen there is already a new foie gras.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'what for, why', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What have you come for?
What's that for?
Oh, Samson. What have you come for?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'только'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: There are so many mistakes there!
I don't have that much time.

examples.text: Там столько ошибок! Мы же всё быстро делали.
examples.trans: There are so many mistakes there! After all, we did everything in a hurry.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to order', paired with 'заказывать'.

examples.trans: Maybe we should order?
We ordered tea and sandwiches.

examples.text: Если опоздают, пицца бесплатно. Может, закажем?
examples.trans: If they're late, the pizza is free. Maybe we should order?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мотреть'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to look, to watch', paired with 'посмотреть'.

examples.trans: Look what I've got.
I'm watching TV.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'already', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been mayor for four years now.
Dad is already home.
I'm already home.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nobody', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Nobody will come in.
I know the town like nobody else.

examples.text: Садитесь и держите дверь. Никто не войдёт.
examples.trans: Sit down and hold the door. Nobody will come in.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'nothing', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There's nothing left.
I don't know anything.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: I want coffee.
If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'at, by; (у меня) I have', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
He's at our place.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'юрприз'). Common masculine noun meaning 'surprise' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I'll show you one surprise.
What surprise?
It was a surprise.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'здравить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to congratulate, to greet', paired with 'поздравлять'.

examples.trans: I want to officially congratulate you.

examples.text: Друзья пришли поздравить Нину с днём рождения.
examples.trans: Friends came to wish Nina a happy birthday.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'our, ours', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town.
This is our flat.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('young').

examples.text: Молодой человек, как на тест-драйв записаться?
examples.trans: Young man, how do I sign up for a test drive?
They have a young family.

examples.text: Молодой человек, а как на тест-драйв записаться?
examples.trans: Young man, how do I sign up for a test drive?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'collective, staff, team' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: The staff forced me into this.

examples.text: У нас на работе очень дружный коллектив.
examples.trans: We have a very friendly team at work.

examples.text: Я своё мнение не менял. Это меня коллектив заставил.
examples.trans: I haven't changed my opinion. The staff forced me into this.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'фессионал'). Common masculine noun meaning 'professional' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He's a real professional.
There's nothing but professionals here.

examples.text: У вас тут в провинции одни профессионалы.
examples.trans: You've got nothing but professionals out here in the provinces.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.trans: They called from the Italian restaurant.
In the evening they went to a restaurant.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'частливый'). Qualitative adjective formed with the productive suffix '-тельный'/'-ливый'. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('happy; lucky').

examples.trans: I'm very happy.
The film has a happy ending.

examples.text: Ты сейчас один против всех. Счастливого конца не будет.
examples.trans: Right now you're alone against everyone. There won't be a happy ending.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'корённый'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('conquered, charmed').

examples.trans: I am happy, conquered by the power.

examples.text: Сегодня у шефа очень покорённый день в ресторане.
examples.trans: Today the chef is having a very conquered day at the restaurant.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'power, government, authorities' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: People need to go into government themselves.

examples.text: Самим идти во власть? Что это значит?
examples.trans: Go into government themselves? What does that mean?
The grandson of a collaborator is clawing his way into power!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: This house.
I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'eye' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я не буду закрывать на это глаза.
examples.trans: I'm not going to close my eyes to this.
She has blue eyes.

examples.text: А я глаза на это закрывать не буду. Я подниму людей!
examples.trans: Well, I'm not going to close my eyes to this. I'll rally people!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'иний'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('blue, dark blue').

examples.trans: Did you find that little blue bottle?
Did you find the vial? That little blue bottle.
That little blue bottle.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'song' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Bellowing songs!
This is my favourite old song.

examples.text: О, это, Аркашенька, бывает очень часто. Песни орём!
examples.trans: Oh, that happens very often, Arkashenka. Bellowing songs!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'she; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: She's a lecturer.
I haven't heard of her.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'просить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to ask', paired with 'спрашивать'.

examples.text: А спросите у него, куда он дел компьютерный класс.
examples.trans: Ask him where he put the computer lab.
May I ask you something?

examples.text: Да? А спросите у него, куда он дел компьютерный класс.
examples.trans: Really? Then ask him where he put the computer lab.
